input:
A temperature measurement provides a convenient means of separating two terms that are too often merged in practice, namely error and uncertainty. The discussion works with one reading and its stated tolerance, and keeps the two terms apart throughout, because a correction that is right for one will generally be wrong for the other.

The reading is 338 units, and the tolerance on the reading is 2% of the reading. It follows that the absolute error works out at 6.76 units. By absolute error is meant the size of the difference between the reading and the true value, expressed in the units of the measurement itself. Relative error, by contrast, means the same difference divided by the reading, expressed as a fraction or as a percentage of the reading; the tolerance is quoted in the relative form, and the worked figure converts the tolerance to the absolute form. The sign also forms part of the definition: the error of a measurement is the reading minus the true value, and a tolerance stated without a sign bounds the error in both directions.

Uncertainty, however, is an altogether different quantity from error. The uncertainty of a measurement states the range within which the true value is believed to lie, given what is known about the instrument and about the measurement as performed. An error is a single difference between a reading and the true value, correctable in principle once known; an uncertainty is a dispersion of the values the measurement could return, reduced by a better instrument or by repeated readings, but not removed by a single subtraction. A reading of 338 units with an absolute error of 6.76 units accordingly reports the measurement and the bound on its error together, and neither figure amounts to an uncertainty statement. The distinction carries a practical consequence: calibration removes a known error, whereas the uncertainty determines the smallest difference between two readings that the measurement can support.
